newsitem.title: USA: MS High Court to hear GM Hughes appeal.
newsitem.headline: MS High Court to hear GM Hughes appeal.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court said Tuesday it would hear an appeal by a unit of General Motors Corp's Hughes Electronics over a whistleblower law that allows individuals to sue for alleged false or fradulent claims involving the U.S. government.

The case stemmed from a lawsuit filed in 1989 by William Schumer, a former manager at Hughes Aircraft Co, alleging the firm mischarged costs from a fixed-price contract for the F-15 aircraft to the cost-reimbursement contract for the B-2 aircraft.
He sought $150 million in damages. The U.S. Justice Department declined to join the civil lawsuit.
A federal judge in California dismissed the lawsuit.

But a U.S. Court of Appeals reinstated the parts of the suit alleging that Hughes failed to properly disclose the terms of its agreements to its customer and did not comply with the disclosure requirements under cost accounting standards.
In its Supreme Court appeal, Hughes argued that the lower courts lacked jurisdiction over the case and that injury to the U.S. Treasury was required for a suit under the federal false claims law.
It also challenged the constitutionality of allowing private individuals to bring such suits for damages against the government.
Supporting the appeal were the U.S. Chamber of Commerce business group and trade associations representing aircraft manufactuers, shipbuilders and the electronics industry.

The Supreme Court said it would consider a 1986 amendment to the law that provides that no court shall have jurisdiction over a whistleblower lawsuit, based on the public disclosure of the allegations in various government hearings or reports or in the news media.

The court agreed to consider if the amendment applies to the Schumer lawsuit, which has filed after the amendment took effect, but alleged violations before 1986. The justices also will consider if any public disclosures occurred in the case.
Hughes Aircraft contended the suit was based on the public disclosure of allegations in an administrative audit.
The Justice Department supported the law as constitutional and urged the high court to reject the company's appeal.
The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments in the case early next year, with a decision due before July.
